'''Leonard Susskind''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|ʌ|s|k|ɪ|n|d}}; born June 16, 1940)<ref name=lennyfest>{{cite web |date = May 20–21, 2000 |url = http://www.stanford.edu/dept/physics/events/lennyfest.html |title = Lennyfest |postscript = : |access-date = 2007-07-01 |archive-date = 2013-10-17 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131017092157/http://www.stanford.edu/dept/physics/events/lennyfest.html |url-status = dead }}his 60th birth anniversary was celebrated with a special symposium at Stanford University.</ref><ref name=santafe>{{cite web |date = June 26, 2013 |url = http://www.santafe.edu/news/item/lecture-susskind-arrow-of-time/ |title = Why is Time a One-Way Street?|work = Santa Fe Institute | postscript = :}}in Geoffrey West's introduction, he gives Suskind's current age as 74 and says his birthday was recent.</ref> is an American theoretical physicist, professor of [[theoretical physics]] at [[Stanford University]] and founding director of the [[Stanford Institute for Theoretical Physics]]. His research interests are [[string theory]], [[quantum field theory]], [[quantum statistical mechanics]] and [[quantum cosmology]].<ref name=StanfordFaculty>{{Cite web |url=http://www.stanford.edu/dept/physics/people/faculty/susskind_leonard.html |title=Faculty information sheet |publisher=Stanford University |access-date=2009-09-01 |archive-date=March 9, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130309031920/http://www.stanford.edu/dept/physics/people/faculty/susskind_leonard.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is a member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{Cite press release |url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=05022000 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070630205856/http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=05022000 |archive-date=June 30, 2007 |date=May 2, 2000 |title=60 New Members Chosen by Academy|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |access-date=2009-09-01}}</ref> and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name=bioAtEdge/> an associate member of the faculty of Canada's [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]],<ref>{{cite news |url = http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/news/leonard-susskind-joins-pi |title = Leonard Susskind Joins PI |date = October 15, 2007 |access-date = December 6, 2012 |archive-date = September 24, 2015 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150924072151/http://www.perimeterinstitute.ca/news/leonard-susskind-joins-pi |url-status = dead }}</ref> and a distinguished professor of the [[Korea Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.kias.re.kr/sub02/sub02_01_01.jsp?empid=MTAwNjc= |publisher = [[Korea Institute for Advanced Study]] |title = Susskind, Leonard: Distinguished Professor / School of Physics: Theoretical Particle Physics |access-date = December 6, 2012 |archive-date = April 20, 2014 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140420081752/http://www.kias.re.kr/sub02/sub02_01_01.jsp?empid=MTAwNjc= |url-status = dead }}</ref>

Susskind is widely regarded as one of the fathers of string theory.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.nyas.org/Publications/Media/PodcastDetail.aspx?cid=2578b7c1-2032-4818-a461-0febfddf2707 |publisher = NYAS Publications |title = Father of String Theory Muses on the Megaverse |access-date = December 2, 2013 |archive-date = December 14, 2014 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141214044154/http://www.nyas.org/Publications/Media/PodcastDetail.aspx?cid=2578b7c1-2032-4818-a461-0febfddf2707 |url-status = dead }}</ref> He was the first to give a precise string-theoretic interpretation of the [[holographic principle]] in 1995<ref name=SusskindArXiv>{{cite journal |title=The World as a Hologram |last=Susskind |first=Leonard |doi=10.1063/1.531249 |date=1995 |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=36 |issue=11 |pages=6377–6396|arxiv=hep-th/9409089 |bibcode = 1995JMP....36.6377S |s2cid=17316840 }}</ref> and the first to introduce the idea of the [[string theory landscape]] in 2003.<ref name="arXiv-0302219">{{Cite journal |arxiv=hep-th/0302219 |author1=Leonard Susskind |title=The Anthropic Landscape of String Theory |journal=The Davis Meeting on Cosmic Inflation |pages=26 |date=2003 |bibcode=2003dmci.confE..26S }}</ref><ref name="SciAm-2011">{{Cite journal |last1 = Byrne |first1 = P. |doi = 10.1038/scientificamerican0711-80 |title = Bad Boy of Physics |journal = Scientific American |volume = 305 |issue = 1 |pages = 80–83 |year = 2011 |url = http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=bad-boy-of-physics |bibcode = 2011SciAm.305f..80B|url-access = subscription }}</ref>

Susskind was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize|1998 J. J. Sakurai Prize]],<ref name=Sakurai/> the [[Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture|2018 Oskar Klein Medal]],<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.okc.albanova.se/research/memorial-lecture | title=The Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture | access-date=February 4, 2019 | archive-date=December 17, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201217082111/http://www.okc.albanova.se/research/memorial-lecture | url-status=dead }}</ref> and the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] of the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in 2023.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Dirac Medallists 2023 {{!}} ICTP |url=https://www.ictp.it/home/dirac-medallists-2023 |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=www.ictp.it}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Leonard Susskind was born in the [[South Bronx]] in New York City to a poor Jewish family whose father was a plumber.<ref name=LATimes2008>{{Cite news |url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2008-jul-26-sci-susskind26-story.html |title = Leonard Susskind discusses duel with Stephen Hawking |newspaper = Los Angeles Times |date = July 26, 2008 |last1 = Johnson |first1 = John Jr }}</ref> He began working as a plumber himself at the age of 16, taking over from his father who had become ill.<ref name=LATimes2008/> Susskind attended [[Bronx High School of Science|The Bronx High School of Science]]. Later, he enrolled in the [[City College of New York]] as an engineering student and had planned to study mechanical engineering but he changed his mind and later graduated with a B.S. in physics in 1962.<ref name=bioAtEdge /> In an interview in the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', Susskind recalls a discussion with his father that changed his career path: "When I told my father I wanted to be a physicist, he said, 'Hell no, you ain't going to work in a drug store.' I said, 'No, not a pharmacist.' I said, 'Like Einstein.' He poked me in the chest with a piece of plumbing pipe. 'You ain't going to be no engineer,' he said. 'You're going to be Einstein.{{'"}}<ref name=LATimes2008/> Susskind then studied at [[Cornell University]] under [[Peter A. Carruthers]], where he earned his Ph.D. in 1965.

== Career ==
[[File:Susskind_at_cornell.jpg|thumb|right|Susskind giving 2014 [[Messenger Lectures|Messenger Lecture]] at Cornell]]

Susskind was an assistant professor of physics, then an associate professor at [[Yeshiva University]] (1966–1970), after which he went for a year to the [[Tel Aviv University]] (1971–72), returning to Yeshiva to become a professor of physics (1970–1979). Since 1979 he has been professor of physics at [[Stanford University]],<ref name=StanfordFaculty/> and since 2000 has held the [[Felix Bloch]] professorship of physics.

Susskind was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize|1998 J. J. Sakurai Prize]] for his "pioneering contributions to hadronic string models, [[Lattice gauge theory|lattice gauge theories]], [[quantum chromodynamics]], and dynamical symmetry breaking." Susskind's hallmark, according to colleagues, has been the application of "brilliant imagination and originality to the theoretical study of the nature of the elementary particles and forces that make up the physical world."<ref name=Sakurai>{{cite press release |url = http://news.stanford.edu/pr/97/971105sakurai.html |title = Susskind wins prestigious Sakurai Prize in theoretical physics |publisher = Stanford University |first = David F. |last = Salisbury |date = 11 May 1997 |access-date = June 20, 2009 |archive-date = May 27, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160527011705/http://news.stanford.edu/pr/97/971105sakurai.html |url-status = dead }}</ref>

In 2007, Susskind joined the faculty of [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Waterloo, [[Ontario]], Canada, as an associate member. He has been elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. He is also a [[distinguished professor]] at [[Korea Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>[http://www.kias.re.kr/en/programs/physics_members_all.jsp Welcome To Kias<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071105002440/http://www.kias.re.kr/en/programs/physics_members_all.jsp |date=2007-11-05 }}</ref>

=== Scientific career ===
Susskind was one of at least three physicists, alongside [[Yoichiro Nambu]] and [[Holger Bech Nielsen]], who independently discovered during or around 1970 that [[Gabriele Veneziano]]'s [[dual resonance model]] of [[strong interactions]] could be described by a quantum mechanical model of oscillating strings,<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=hep-th/0007118|author1=Schwarz|title=String Theory: The Early Years|date=2000 }}<!-- [http://www.arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/0007118 String Theory: The Early Years], John H. Schwarz, 2000 --></ref> and was the first to propose the idea of the [[string theory landscape]]. Susskind has also made important contributions in the following areas of physics:
* The independent discovery of the string theory model of particle physics<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Susskind |first1 = L |year = 1969 |title = Structure of hadrons implied by duality |journal = Physical Review D |volume = 1 |issue = 4 |pages = 1182–1186 |doi=10.1103/physrevd.1.1182 |bibcode = 1970PhRvD...1.1182S}}</ref>
* The theory of [[quark]] [[colour confinement|confinement]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1 = Susskind |first1 = L. |author-link = Leonard Susskind |title = Lattice models of quark confinement at high temperature |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.20.2610 |journal = [[Physical Review D]] |volume = 20 |issue = 10 |pages = 2610–2618 |year = 1979 |bibcode = 1979PhRvD..20.2610S |osti = 1446781 }}</ref>
* The development of [[Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory]] known as [[staggered fermion|Kogut–Susskind fermions]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1 = Kogut |first1 = John|last2 = Susskind |first2 = Leonard |author-link2 = Leonard Susskind |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.11.395 |title = Hamiltonian formulation of Wilson's lattice gauge theories |journal = [[Physical Review D]]| volume = 11 |issue = 2 |pages = 395 |year = 1975 |bibcode = 1975PhRvD..11..395K}}</ref>
* The theory of scaling violations in deep inelastic electroproduction
* The theory of symmetry breaking sometimes known as "[[technicolor (physics)|technicolor]] theory"<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yao |first1=W. -M. |year=2006 |title=Review of Particle Physics |journal=[[Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics]] |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=1–1232 |arxiv=astro-ph/0601168 |bibcode=2006JPhG...33....1Y |doi=10.1088/0954-3899/33/1/001}}
*Dynamical Electroweak Symmetry Breaking section cites two 1979 publications, one by [[Steven Weinberg]], the other by L. Susskind to represent the earliest models with technicolor and technifermions. [http://pdg.lbl.gov/2007/reviews/color_s057.pdf]</ref>
* The second, yet independent, theory of cosmological [[baryogenesis]]<ref>[http://www.aps.org/units/dpf/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Leonard&last_nm=Susskind&year=1998 Biography], [[American Physical Society]] website (last accessed November, 2013)</ref> ([[Andrei Sakharov]]'s work was first, but was mostly unknown in the Western hemisphere)
* String theory of [[black hole]] entropy<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=hep-th/9309145|author1=Leonard Susskind|title=Some Speculations about Black Hole Entropy in String Theory|date=1993 }}<!-- L. Susskind, RU-93-44, [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9309145 hep-th/9309145]. --></ref>
* The principle of [[black hole complementarity]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1 = Susskind |first1 = L. |author-link1 = Leonard Susskind| title = String theory and the principle of black hole complementarity |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2367 |journal = [[Physical Review Letters]]| volume = 71 |issue = 15 |pages = 2367–2368 |year = 1993 |pmid = 10054662|arxiv = hep-th/9307168|bibcode = 1993PhRvL..71.2367S |s2cid = 18516175 }}</ref>
* The [[causal patch]] hypothesis
* The [[holographic principle]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1 = Bousso |first1 = R. |author-link1 = Raphael Bousso |title = The holographic principle |doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.74.825 |journal = [[Reviews of Modern Physics]] |volume = 74 |issue = 3 |pages = 825–874 |year = 2002 |arxiv = hep-th/0203101|bibcode = 2002RvMP...74..825B |s2cid = 55096624 }}{{blockquote|The insistence on unitarity in the presence of black holes led 't Hooft (1993) and Susskind (1995b) to embrace a more radical, ''holographic'' interpretation of ...}}</ref>
* [[M-theory]], including development of the Banks–Fischler–Shenker–Susskind [[Matrix string theory|matrix string model]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1 = Banks |first1 = T. |last2 = Fischler |first2 = W. |last3 = Shenker |first3 = S. H. |last4 = Susskind |first4 = L.|title = M theory as a matrix model: A conjecture |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.55.5112 |journal = [[Physical Review D]]| volume = 55 |issue = 8 |pages = 5112–5128 |year = 1997 |arxiv = hep-th/9610043 |bibcode = 1997PhRvD..55.5112B |citeseerx = 10.1.1.268.5260 |s2cid = 13073785 }}</ref>
* Introduction of holographic [[entropy]] bounds in [[physical cosmology]]
* Cool horizons for entangled black holes
* The idea of an [[Anthropic principle|anthropic]] [[string theory landscape]]<ref name="arXiv-0302219"/>
* The [[FRW/CFT duality|census taker's hat]]
* Most recently, application of ideas from information and computation theory, such as the [[CA-duality|complexity equals action conjecture]], to the physics and thermodynamics of black holes, and holographic theories in general.

==Books==
Susskind is the author of several popular science books.

===''The Cosmic Landscape''===
{{Main|The Cosmic Landscape}}
''The Cosmic Landscape: String Theory and the Illusion of Intelligent Design'' is Susskind's first popular science book, published by Little, Brown and Company on December 12, 2005.<ref name="CosmicLandscapeBook">{{Cite book |author=L. Susskind |url=https://archive.org/details/cosmiclandscapes00suss |title=The Cosmic Landscape: String Theory and the Illusion of Intelligent Design |date=2005 |publisher=Little, Brown |isbn=978-0-316-15579-3 |url-access=registration}} [https://www.amazon.com/Cosmic-Landscape-String-Illusion-Intelligent/dp/0316013331]</ref> It is Susskind's attempt to bring his idea of the anthropic landscape of string theory to the general public. In the book, Susskind describes how the string theory landscape was an almost inevitable consequence of several factors, one of which was [[Steven Weinberg]]'s prediction of the [[cosmological constant]] in 1987. The question addressed here is why our universe is fine-tuned for our existence. Susskind explains that Weinberg calculated that if the cosmological constant was just a little different, our universe would cease to exist.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

===''The Black Hole War''===
{{Main|The Black Hole War|Susskind–Hawking battle}}

''The Black Hole War: My Battle with [[Stephen Hawking]] to Make the World Safe for Quantum Mechanics'' is Susskind's second popular science book, published by Little, Brown, and Company on July 7, 2008.<ref name="BlackHoleWarBook">{{Cite book |author=L. Susskind |title=The Black Hole War: My battle with Stephen Hawking to make the world safe for quantum mechanics |date=2008 |publisher=Little, Brown |isbn=978-0-316-01640-7}} [https://www.amazon.com/Black-Hole-War-Stephen-Mechanics/dp/0316016403]</ref> The book is his most famous work and explains what he thinks would happen to the information and matter stored in a black hole when it evaporates. The book sparked from a debate that started in 1981, when there was a meeting of physicists to try to decode some of the mysteries about how particles of particular elemental compounds function. During this discussion Stephen Hawking stated that the information inside a black hole is lost forever as the black hole evaporates. It took 28 years for Leonard Susskind to formulate his theory that would prove Hawking wrong. He then published his theory in his book, ''The Black Hole War''. Like ''The Cosmic Landscape'', ''The Black Hole War'' is aimed at the lay reader. He writes: "The real tools for understanding the quantum universe are abstract mathematics: infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces, projection operators, unitary matrices and a lot of other advanced principles that take a few years to learn. But let's see how we do in just a few pages".{{cn|date=July 2026}}

===''The Theoretical Minimum'' book series===
{{main|The Theoretical Minimum}}
Susskind co-authored a series of companion books to his lecture series [[#The Theoretical Minimum lecture series|''The Theoretical Minimum'']]. The first of these, ''[[The Theoretical Minimum|The Theoretical Minimum: What You Need to Know to Start Doing Physics]]'',<ref name=TTMClassicalMechanicsBook>{{Cite book|last1=Susskind|first1=Leonard|last2=Hrabovsky|first2=George|title=The Theoretical Minimum: What You Need to Know to Start Doing Physics|publisher=Basic Books|date=2013|isbn=978-0-465-02811-5|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/theoreticalminim0000suss}}</ref> was published in 2013 and presents the modern formulations of classical mechanics. The second of these, ''Quantum Mechanics: The Theoretical Minimum'',<ref name=TTMQuantumMechanicsBook>{{Cite book| last1=Susskind |first1=Leonard |last2=Friedman |first2=Art |title=Quantum Mechanics: The Theoretical Minimum|publisher=Basic Books|date=2014|isbn=978-0-465-03667-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_b7WAgAAQBAJ}}</ref> was published in February 2014. The third book, ''Special Relativity and Classical Field Theory: The Theoretical Minimum'' (September 26, 2017),<ref>{{Cite book| last1=Susskind |first1=Leonard |last2=Friedman |first2=Art |title=Special Relativity and Classical Field Theory: The Theoretical Minimum|publisher=Basic Books|date=2017|isbn=978-0465093342 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ukjTDQAAQBAJ}}</ref> introduces readers to Einstein's special relativity and Maxwell's classical field theory. The fourth book in the series, ''General Relativity: The Theoretical Minimum'' was published in January 2023.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Susskind |first1=Leonard |title=General relativity: the theoretical minimum |last2=Cabannes |first2=André François |date=2023 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-1-5416-0177-2 |edition=First |location=New York, NY}}</ref>

==''The Theoretical Minimum'' lecture series==
Susskind teaches a series of Stanford Continuing Studies courses about modern physics referred to as ''[[The Theoretical Minimum]]''. The title of the series is a clear reference to [[Lev Landau|Landau]]'s famous comprehensive exam called the "Theoretical Minimum" which students were expected to pass before admission to his school. ''The Theoretical Minimum'' lectures later formed the basis for the books of the same name.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gribbin |first1=John |title=Physics Made (Almost) Easy |url=https://online.wsj.com/news/articles/SB10001424127887323968304578250253842601938|access-date=4 June 2014 |work=[[Wall Street Journal]] |date=1 February 2013}}</ref> The goal of the courses is to teach the basic but rigorous theoretical foundations required to study certain areas of physics. The sequence covers [[classical mechanics]], [[Theory of relativity|relativity]], [[quantum mechanics]], [[statistical mechanics]], and [[physical cosmology|cosmology]], including the physics of [[black holes]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Theoretical Minimum |url=http://theoreticalminimum.com/home |website=theoreticalminimum.com|access-date=3 June 2014}}</ref>

These courses are available on ''The Theoretical Minimum'' website, on [[iTunes]], and on [[YouTube]]. The courses are intended for the mathematically literate<ref>{{cite journal | title=Physics: Inside utter strangeness| date=2014-02-26| doi=10.1038/506431a| last1=Seery| first1=David| journal=Nature| volume=506| issue=7489| page=431| bibcode=2014Natur.506..431S| s2cid=4464751| doi-access=free}}</ref> public as well as physical science/mathematics students. Susskind aims the courses at people with prior exposure to algebra, and calculus.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Theoretical Minimum|url=http://theoreticalminimum.com/|access-date=12 June 2014|quote=The courses are specifically aimed at people who know, or once knew, a bit of algebra and calculus, but are more or less beginners.}}</ref> Homework and study outside of class is otherwise unnecessary. Susskind explains most of the mathematics used, which form the basis of the lectures.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

==Cornell Messenger Lectures==
Susskind gave 3 lectures "[https://web.archive.org/web/20140706042615/http://www.cornell.edu/video/playlist/leonard-susskind-messenger-lectures The Birth of the Universe and the Origin of Laws of Physics]" April 28-May 1, 2014 in the Cornell [[Messenger Lectures|Messenger Lecture]] series which are posted on a Cornell website.<ref>{{Cite web|title = The Birth of the Universe and the Origin of Laws of Physics - CornellCast|url = https://www.cornell.edu/video/playlist/leonard-susskind-messenger-lectures|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140706042615/http://www.cornell.edu/video/playlist/leonard-susskind-messenger-lectures|url-status = dead|archive-date = July 6, 2014|website = CornellCast|access-date = 2015-12-26}}</ref>

==Smolin–Susskind debate<!--'Smolin–Susskind debate' redirects here-->==
The '''Smolin–Susskind debate'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> refers to the series of intense postings in 2004 between [[Lee Smolin]] and Susskind, concerning Smolin's argument that the "''[[anthropic principle]]'' cannot yield any falsifiable predictions, and therefore cannot be a part of science".<ref name=EdgeSmolinSusskind>{{cite web |title=Smolin vs. Susskind: The anthropic principle |publisher=[[Edge Institute]] |date=August 2004 |series=3rd&nbsp;Culture |website=edge.org |url=http://edge.org/3rd_culture/smolin_susskind04/smolin_susskind.html |access-date=2009-09-01 |df=dmy-all}}</ref> It began on July 26, 2004, with Smolin's publication of "scientific alternatives to the anthropic principle".{{citation needed|date=October 2024}} Smolin e-mailed Susskind asking for a comment. Having not had the chance to read the paper, Susskind requested a summarization of his arguments.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

Smolin obliged, and on July 28, 2004, Susskind responded, saying that the logic Smolin followed "can lead to ridiculous conclusions".<ref name=EdgeSmolinSusskind/> The next day, Smolin responded, saying that "If a large body of our colleagues feels comfortable believing a theory that cannot be proved wrong, then the progress of science could get stuck, leading to a situation in which false, but unfalsifiable theories dominate the attention of our field." This was followed by another paper by Susskind which made a few comments about Smolin's theory of "cosmic natural selection".<ref>{{cite web |title=Letter from Leonard Susskind |website=cohesion.rice.edu |publisher=[[Rice University]] |access-date=2009-06-24 |url-status=dead |url=http://cohesion.rice.edu/CampusServices/OWeek/emplibrary/letterfromleonardsusskind.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021175504/http://cohesion.rice.edu/CampusServices/OWeek/emplibrary/letterfromleonardsusskind.pdf |archive-date=21 October 2012 }}</ref>

The Smolin–Susskind debate finally ended with each of them agreeing to write a final letter which would be posted on the edge.org website, with three conditions attached:
: (1) No more than one letter each.
: (2) Neither sees the other's letter in advance.
: (3) No changes after the fact.

== Personal life ==
He has been married twice, first in 1960,<ref name=bioAtEdge>[http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/susskind.html www.edge.org] • ''Leonard Susskind - A Biography'' (last accessed August 12, 2007).</ref> and has four children.<ref>{{cite news|title=The man who proved Stephen Hawking wrong|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/10654762/The-man-who-proved-Stephen-Hawking-wrong.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/10654762/The-man-who-proved-Stephen-Hawking-wrong.html |archive-date=2022-01-12 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|access-date=16 October 2016|work=Telegraph.co.uk}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

== Further reading ==
* Chown, Marcus, [https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg20126911.300-our-world-may-be-a-giant-hologram.html "Our world may be a giant hologram"], ''[[New Scientist]]'', 15 January 2009, issue 2691: "The holograms you find on credit cards and banknotes are etched on two-dimensional plastic films. When light bounces off them, it recreates the appearance of a 3D image. In the 1990s physicists Leonard Susskind and Nobel prize winner [[Gerard 't Hooft]] suggested that the same principle might apply to the universe as a whole. Our everyday experience might itself be a holographic projection of physical processes that take place on a distant, 2D surface."
